quote: My books are packed up for the move, but I believe that one experiment showed that a shift from 100% probability to 99% probability weighed larger in people’s minds than a shift from 80% probability to 20% probability.
content: No experiment is cited, and the claim contradicts the best-known estimates. Take Tversky & Kahneman (1992)'s fitted weighting function for gains. The drop in decision weight from 100% to 99% is about 0.09; the drop from 80% to 20% is about 0.35, roughly four times larger. The certainty effect is real: the last percentage point weighs more than its face value. It does not weigh more than a sixty-point swing. The essay's "one time's certainty is another time's probability" argument rests on a misremembered size.

quote: If $24,000 would double your existing assets, pick A.
content: This arithmetic is wrong. With logarithmic utility and $24,000 of existing assets, option A gives ln(48,000) ≈ 10.779. Option B gives (33/34)·ln(51,000) + (1/34)·ln(24,000) ≈ 10.817. Log utility picks B. It favors A only if existing assets are below roughly $550. Applied to its own worked example, the essay's recommended procedure gives the opposite of the answer it states.

quote: Oh, and be sure to assess the utility of total asset values—the utility of final outcome states of the world—not changes in assets, or you’ll end up inconsistent again.
content: Rabin (2000)'s calibration theorem shows what this advice costs. Suppose an expected-utility maximizer over total wealth always turns down a 50–50 bet to lose $100 or gain $110. Then it must also turn down a 50–50 bet to lose $1,000 or gain any sum at all, however large. Nearly everyone shows modest risk aversion over small stakes, and that is incompatible with expected utility of final wealth. It is a major reason behavioral economists moved to utility measured relative to a reference point, the approach this sentence forbids.

quote: You cannot feed a probability of 1 into a utility function. It makes no sense.
content: It makes sense once outcomes are described fully. If losing the gamble includes the regret of having passed up a sure $24,000, that outcome differs from simply receiving nothing. A utility function over such outcomes can then rationalize the Allais pattern without "feeding in" a probability; that is regret theory (Loomes & Sugden 1982). Whether regret belongs in the outcome is a substantive question about how outcomes should be described (Broome, Weighing Goods, 1991; book, no DOI), and "fundamentally different types" answers it by decree. "High Challenge" relies on the opposite answer when it values processes as well as end states.

quote: On one occasion, gamblers in Las Vegas played these kinds of bets for real money, using a roulette wheel.
content: The Las Vegas study is Lichtenstein & Slovic (1973), not the 1971 laboratory study the footnote cites first, and the transcript is sourced secondhand, through a popular book and an edited collection. Tversky, Slovic & Kahneman (1990, American Economic Review; no DOI) later traced these reversals mainly to how prices are asked for: people overprice long-shot bets when asked for a dollar figure. They are not mainly intransitive preferences. And when subjects face real arbitrage in market-like settings, reversals shrink quickly (Chu & Chu 1990, American Economic Review; no DOI). The one gambler who shrugged is vivid, but the research shows that most people who are exploited repeatedly stop.

quote: But what if it were 24,000 lives at stake, instead of $24,000? The certainty effect is even stronger over human lives.
content: No study is cited for "even stronger over human lives," and life-saving versions of these problems differ from money versions in ways that matter. Distribution and fairness bear on choices about lives: whether the risk falls on everyone or on identifiable people, whether some are certain to die. Many people and many ethical theories care about these things (Diamond 1967). Treating the certainty preference over lives as the same bias magnified skips the question of whether it is a bias at all.
